newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Investment, not aid, key to Africa growth - Summer.
newsitem.headline: Investment, not aid, key to Africa growth - Summer.

text.p: Economic growth in Africa will be achieved by making the continent more attractive for trade and investment, not by pouring more aid, U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said on Tuesday.
Summers told an African Development Bank (AfDB) seminar, aid to states pursuing bad policies could even be counter-productive.
"Without political stability, macroeconomic control and reasonably functioning markets, aid is at best ineffective," he said.
Aid that was not carefully targetted might crowd out private investment and allow governments to postpone painful steps necessary to gain credibility, Summers said.
It could lead to overvalued exchange rates that hampered exports and to unsustainable debt burdens, he added.

"More aid cannot be the key to sustainable rapid growth in Africa," Summers said. "Instead, what we have seen around the world is that countries prosper when they earn their external resources by adding value and exporting, or by creating an alluring environment for private capital."
That belief underpins the recent U.S. government initiative to promote trade and investment in Africa.
Summers said this was not just "another donor-inspired Africa Initiative".
"Rather, it is our response to the initiatives that African governments are taking," he said.
The symposium was held the day before the African Development Bank starts its three-day annual meeting here.
The big theme this year is how to attract private sector investment. The AfDB estimates that less than three percent of foreign direct private investment comes to Africa.

The AfDB itself -- a much reformed organisation under its president of almost two years, Omar Kabbaj -- is developing its work with the private sector, while remaining a development bank geared towards reducing poverty.
Kabbaj implored African governments not to be discouraged by the lack of interest shown hitherto by investors.
"Clearly, the slower than expected response of private sector investment should not lead to the abandonment of reform measures," Kabbaj said.
"It should instead lead to a renewed commitment and to their further deepening. These are essential to garner the required credibility."
Summers said the U.S. government would back up its trade initiative by holding annual ministerial-level meetings "with selected African countries undertaking bold reforms".
